revisions.title: Ion's asymmetry becomes Socrates' test
revisions.body: Ion names the puzzle: other poets make him drowsy, while Homer gives him fluency. Socrates turns that asymmetry into a test, proposing that knowledge of a whole craft should extend across its practitioners; he illustrates the proposal through painting, sculpture, and music. One way to read these analogies is as pressure on Ion’s claim, not proof that poetry must work exactly like those crafts. Ion returns to his Homeric excellence.

revisions.title: Authority on loan
revisions.body: The crucial move here is to change the question from how Ion performs to where his authority comes from. Socrates presents poetic excellence as something transmitted through divine inspiration, so the poet appears as an interpreter rather than an independent maker. Tynnichus is offered as a striking illustration of that proposal, not as a conclusive proof.

revisions.title: The Proteus escape: from general to divine
revisions.body: Ion says that Ephesus—not Athens—needs no general because it is ruled and commanded by Athens; he says Athens and Sparta reject him because they regard themselves as sufficient. Socrates answers with foreign generals Athens has chosen, then recasts Ion’s evasions as Protean shape-shifting. The final choice is narrow: if Ion has an art, he is unjust; if divinely possessed, he is not. Ion chooses “divine,” and Socrates grants him that label.
